MEAA mourns the passing of legendary music journalist, broadcaster, author and long-time MEAA member Glenn A. Baker, who joined MEAA in 1979. A towering figure in Australian music journalism, Glenn's passion, knowledge and storytelling helped shape the nation's understanding of popular music for more than five decades. From his role in the early days of double j, to his work as a broadcaster, author, record label founder and long-time Billboard editor, his influence on Australia's music culture was immeasurable.

Glenn was renowned for his encyclopaedic music knowledge, championing of Australian artists, and unwavering enthusiasm for sharing stories about music with audiences around the world.

 Our thoughts are with his family, friends, colleagues and the many musicians, journalists and music lovers whose lives he touched.

Australia's live performance industry is in crisis. Production cancellations are leaving performers, musicians, crew, technicians and creative workers without work, and audiences and communities across Australia are also losing out.

Without urgent action, we risk losing the talent, skills and creativity that make Australia's live performance sector thrive. Add your voice to the campaign to protect Australia's live performance industry.

"For me, responsible and ethical use of AI starts with respect, for the artists, writers, performers, musicians and creatives whose work has been used to train these systems. If AI is benefiting from the creative output of artists, then artists should know about it, have a choice in it, and be fairly compensated for it." - Leah Purcell, AM

Leah Purcell, AM, is an internationally acclaimed actor, writer, director and producer of stage and screen and a proud Goa-Gunggari-Wakka Wakka Murri woman from Queensland, Australia.

Join Leah Purcell and show your support for our Pay Up campaign. meaa.io/PayUp 
#StopAITheft #PayUp #StrongerTogether

Last weekend MEAA hosted 'Child's Play: developing a lifelong love for arts and culture in Australia' at the ALP National Conference in Adelaide. The event demonstrated why governments across Australia should adopt the principle of lifelong participation in the arts as a core part of cultural policy.

Arabana and Yawuru man Nathan May was joined by the Australian Youth Orchestra (AYO) String Quartet for a performance of 'Wangkarda', and supported composer, conductor and educator Annie Kwok in an interactive music session for attendees.

Former AYO CEO Colin Cornish spoke about the importance of music education, highlighting the vital role the arts play in young people's lives.

#NationalCulturalPolicy @australianyouthorchestra
